passage:
Monday: Pema played football through the whole break in the blazing sun. Her water bottle stayed full in her bag. By maths her head throbbed, and when Samir borrowed her ruler she snapped, "Just take it!" and put her head on the desk. At home Mummy asked, "Did you drink anything today?" Pema thought hard. "Umm. No."
Wednesday: Pema made a rule: a sip at every whistle. Samir laughed, then copied her.
Friday: After a hard match, Pema noticed her mouth was dry and a small ache was starting behind her eyes. She drank before anyone reminded her. In maths she was cheerful, and she even lent Samir her ruler without being asked.

qa.q: What rule did Pema make on Wednesday?
What was Pema feeling in maths on Monday?
qa.a: She felt achy, tired and grumpy, which is why she snapped at Samir.

qa.q: What changed by Friday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Pema noticed her dry mouth and the starting ache and drank without a reminder, so she is learning to read her own body.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt when Pema snapped on Monday?
qa.a: Samir was probably surprised or a bit hurt, not knowing that Pema was thirsty and headachy.

grounding: Shows a child who forgets to drink while playing hard in the sun feeling headachy and grumpy, then learning to notice thirst and carry a bottle.

passage: Tarun, when your Dida was your age in Kolkata, I, Bidisha, played kho-kho in the school yard till my plaits were soaked. I never drank a drop; water was for babies, I thought. One April afternoon I came back to class with a pounding head and legs like wet rope. I shouted at my best friend Mitali for humming, then cried over a spelling test. Our games teacher, Mrs Ghosh, looked at my cracked lips and sat me under the neem tree with her own tin mug of water. "Your body was asking, and you weren't listening," she said. Next morning I carried a brass bottle to school, and I have carried one ever since.

qa.q: Where did Mrs Ghosh sit Bidisha?
What was young Bidisha feeling back in class that afternoon?
qa.a: She felt achy, drained and irritable, so she shouted at Mitali and then cried over a spelling test.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Bidisha's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Mrs Ghosh noticing the cracked lips and giving her water; it taught Bidisha to listen to thirst, and she began carrying a bottle.

qa.q: How might Mitali have felt when Bidisha shouted about the humming?
qa.a: Mitali was probably hurt and puzzled, since the humming was harmless and the anger came from Bidisha's thirst.

grounding: Illustrates a child playing hard in the sun without drinking becoming headachy and grumpy, then learning to notice thirst and carry a bottle.
